source.title: Training neural networks on data sources with unknown reliability
source.authors: A. Capstick; Francesca Palermo; Tian-Yu Cui; P. Barnaghi

record.file_problem: Supplied full text; no file problem noted.
record.tranche_reason: The authors use the premise that networks learn clean patterns before fitting noisy examples to motivate LAP, a method for training on sources with mixed reliability. Their experiments report test performance for that method and its baselines, but do not test any listed claim version.
record.gate_note: The authors describe memorization of noisy examples as motivation and report that standard training can overfit noisy data late in training. Their results compare LAP with baselines on mixtures of clean and noisy sources; they do not measure random-label memorization capacity, the clean-data training–test gap in the listed versions, or the other version-specific outcomes.
record.test_reason: LAP uses the premise that networks learn clean patterns before memorizing noise. Its experiments evaluate training with sources of differing reliability; none measures the comparisons or joint outcomes specified by V1–V8. Partially corrupted training sets and clean-test accuracy do not establish V1's coexistence of near-perfect random-label fitting and natural-label generalization.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors conclude that LAP improves performance with mixtures of reliable and unreliable sources while maintaining performance on noise-free data, across several tasks and modalities.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains with source-specific loss weighting (LAP) to address mixed-reliability data; the listed claim versions concern memorization capacity, architecture, optimizer, batch size, dropout, sharpness, and example removal.
record.method_sensitivity: Noise type, number of noisy sources, and noise level; the authors also report sensitivity to LAP's depression strength, history length, and leniency.

fits_no_version.finding: Standard training retains substantial clean-test performance with selected sources corrupted by random labels or input noise.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Networks can learn useful predictive patterns from mixtures of clean and corrupted sources; performance depends on the dataset and corruption setting.

fits_no_version.finding: On corrupted ImageNet, standard training reaches maximum test top-5 accuracy of 68.05 ± 0.26%, but averages 42.96 ± 0.64% over the final ten epochs. Appendix A.18 interprets the learning curves as late fitting to noise.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Continued training on mixed clean and corrupted sources can reduce clean-test accuracy after an earlier peak.

record.problems: The reported maximum test accuracy is not accompanied by training error, so the train–test gap cannot be calculated. The main comparison uses synthetic noise in selected sources; the text notes that source noise uniform across sources provides no additional source information and LAP then performs as well as standard training.
record.rows_left_out: Other baseline and LAP values in Tables 1–5 and 9–13, plus additional noise/source sweeps and parameter sensitivity results, were left out because they report the performance of the study's proposed LAP method or broader noisy-data results rather than testing a listed claim version. Figure-only curves were also not transcribed.

untested.parts: Near-perfect fitting of fixed random labels, natural-label held-out generalization under the same recipe, and chance held-out accuracy after fully random-label training.
Test error as width increases beyond the width needed for zero training error.
Matched comparisons of convolutional and fully connected image classifiers, including local connectivity and initialization.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under specified tuning budgets and recovery recipes.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and recipe adaptations that reduce them.
Dropout versus no dropout, including training-set size, dropout strength, and augmentation interactions.
Magnitude-aware sharpness, its association with generalization gaps, and comparisons with other measures.
Retraining after removing highly memorized examples versus removing equally many random examples.

record.verdict_notes: Figure 9 does report training cross-entropy loss, so training performance is not entirely unreported. It does not establish near-perfect random-label fitting or the outcomes required by V1. Its LAP loss is tempered and therefore is not directly comparable to standard training loss. The omitted method comparisons and noise sweeps do not supply tests of V1–V8.

versions.untested_parts: Does not measure training accuracy on fixed random labels or compare held-out accuracy for fully random-label and natural-label training.
Does not sweep width beyond the interpolation threshold or report the specified test-error pattern.
Does not compare convolutional and fully connected networks on the stated architectural question.
Does not compare adaptive optimizers with SGD on the optimizer generalization claim.
Does not vary batch size to test its effect on the generalization gap.
Does not vary dropout to test its effect on held-out error.
Does not measure magnitude-aware sharpness or compare generalization measures.
Does not remove memorized training examples and retrain.

rows.note: Mean ± standard deviation over 5 repeats; this is a noisy-source setting, not the listed natural-label generalization test.

rows.note: Mean ± standard deviation over 5 repeats; this is a noisy-source setting.
